'''''Amaranthus graecizans''''', the '''Mediterranean amaranth'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=AMGR13|taxon=Amaranthus graecizans|accessdate=7 January 2016}}</ref> or '''short-tepalled pigweed''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref> is an annual species in the botanical family [[Amaranthaceae]]. It is native to [[Africa]], southern [[Europe]], [[East Asia]] to [[India]] and [[Central Asia]].<ref>{{cite web |title=''Amaranthus graecizans'' |publisher=Flora of Pakistan |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=5&taxon_id=242415677 |accessdate=2016-04-25}}</ref> It is [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] in North America.  More general [[common name]]s include '''tumbleweed''' and '''pigweed'''.<ref "name=Lyons1900">{{cite book
|title=Plant Names, Scientific and Popular: Including in the Case of Each Plant the Correct Botanical Name in Accordance with the Reformed Nomenclature, Together with Botanical and Popular Synonyms

==Description==
''Amaranthus graecizans'' is an [[annual herb]] that grows up to {{convert|50|cm|abbr=off}} tall. Stems are branched from base, [[glabrousness|glabrous]] or covered with crisped hairs.  The flowers are [[unisexual]] and are yellow with round black seeds that are 1–1.25 mm.<ref>{{cite book|last1=G. Miller|first1=Anthony|last2=Morris|first2=Miranda|title=Plants of Dhofar|date=1988|location=Oman|publisher=Office of the Adviser for Conservation of the Environment, Diwan of Royal Court, Sultanate of Oman|isbn=071570808-2|page=22}}</ref>

==Habitat==
''Amaranthus graecizans'' grows in warm [[temperate zones]] where it can be found at [[elevation]]s up to {{convert|2400|m|ft|-2|abbr=off}}.<ref>{{cite web|title=Amaranthus graecizans|url=http://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Amaranthus+graecizans|website=Useful Tropical Plants|accessdate=24 January 2018}}</ref>  It grows rapidly after rain and can be found on [[disturbed ground]] in the vicinity of human and livestock settlements as well as seasonally flooded sandy flats.<ref>{{cite book|last1=G. Miller|first1=Anthony|last2=Morris|first2=Miranda|title=Plants of Dhofar|date=1988|location=Oman|publisher=Office of the Adviser for Conservation of the Environment, Diwan of Royal Court, Sultanate of Oman|isbn=071570808-2|page=22}}</ref>

==Uses==
The edible leaves are used as a vegetable throughout [[Africa]] and the [[Middle East]].<ref name="prota">Grubben, G.J.H. & Denton, O.A. (2004) Plant Resources of Tropical Africa 2. Vegetables. PROTA Foundation, Wageningen; Backhuys, Leiden; CTA, Wageningen.</ref>  It can be eaten raw, but was more often cooked, or added to sauces and stews.  A common way to cook ''Amaranthus graecizans'' was to cook it in [[buttermilk]], or to squeeze fresh [[Lime (fruit)|lime]]-juice over it.<ref>{{cite book|last1=G. Miller|first1=Anthony|last2=Morris|first2=Miranda|title=Plants of Dhofar|date=1988|location=Oman|publisher=Office of the Adviser for Conservation of the Environment, Diwan of Royal Court, Sultanate of Oman|isbn=071570808-2|page=22}}</ref>  The seeds are [[starch]]y and can also be eaten<ref>{{cite web|title=Amaranthus graecizans|url=http://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Amaranthus+graecizans|website=Useful Tropical Plants|accessdate=24 January 2018}}</ref>
